tour.title: From Death to Resurrection: What the New Testament Hopes For
tour.intro: This tour follows the New Testament’s sequence rather than treating “going to heaven” and resurrection as interchangeable: Jesus’ bodily resurrection, the believer’s presence with Jesus after death, the future raising and transformation of the body, and the final renewal of creation. The teachers sometimes move from biblical text into interpretation, so listen for both what the passages say and how each speaker connects them.

steps.why: Begin here for the basic category distinction. Wright argues from the empty tomb and Jesus’ appearances that “only empty tomb plus appearances will do the trick” of physical resurrection, then says resurrection “is not about somebody going into a glorious angelic state” or simply “going to heaven.” His discussion of Jesus being recognized by the wounds gives the bodily claim a concrete shape without pretending to explain every property of the risen body.
steps.episodeTitle: #164 Easter questions on the resurrection of Jesus

steps.why: This clip gives you a useful two-stage map. Reading Psalm 49 and Peter’s use of Psalm 16 in Acts 2, the speakers describe rescue from death as “a resurrection hope” and say, “It’s not afterlife, it’s more life.” They then distinguish the New Testament’s hope of being with Jesus after death—“today you’ll be with me in paradise”—from the later resurrection life, which they call “the life after the life after death.”
steps.episodeTitle: Nephesh / Soul E3: What Happens After We Die?

steps.why: Now hear the immediate state set beside the final hope in the discussion of 2 Corinthians 5. The commentator says that if death tears down the present “earthly tent,” the believer is still “at home with the Lord,” while carefully adding, “our ultimate hope is resurrection.” This is the clearest stop in the tour for the distinction between what happens at death and what happens at the resurrection.

This supplies Paul’s meaning of “spiritual body,” a phrase that can sound like disembodiment. The speaker reads 1 Corinthians 15 and insists, “It’s just a different kind of embodiment,” and, “You don’t go from a body to a non body.” The seed, perishable/imperishable, glory, and power language helps you hear transformation as continuity-plus-change rather than the soul escaping the body.
steps.episodeTitle: Naked Bible 88: What is the “spiritual body” Paul talks about in 1 Cor 15?

steps.why: This is the New Testament’s climactic body passage in the tour. The commentator walks through Paul’s “last trumpet”: “the dead will be raised imperishable,” the mortal “must put on immortality,” and death is finally swallowed up in victory. It gathers the earlier distinctions into the answer to your central question: the Christian hope is not merely survival after death but a future bodily transformation.

End with the destination toward which resurrection points. Interpreting 2 Peter 3 alongside Revelation 21 and Ephesians 1:10, the speaker describes “new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells,” with “heaven and earth” fully united and God dwelling among humanity. This gives the bodily resurrection its New Testament setting: not permanent disembodied existence, but life in God’s renewed creation.
steps.episodeTitle: New Heavens and New Earth (Part One)

tour.closing: Taken together, these clips present “heaven” as a shorthand some Christians use for being with Jesus after death, but not as the New Testament’s final word about human destiny. The final hope they emphasize is resurrection: God raises and transforms the body, defeats death, and brings creation into its renewed fullness.

caveats: Clips on ad-inserted hosts (Megaphone: ask-nt-wright, spoken-gospel) can land up to ~2 minutes off against today’s stream. This is a known corpus-wide drift, not a bug in this tour.
A tour is model output over machine transcripts. The "why" text should report what a transcript says; it is not a claim that the speaker is right.

The player streams each episode straight from its publisher. A few hosts (Substack’s CDN, for one) refuse hotlinked requests and the step will say so and offer the URL instead — the clip boundaries are still good, the playback path is not.
